CausalChain: CTNNB1 mutation in HepG2 cells -> Impaired HNF4α signaling -> Immature hepatocyte phenotype with low CYP expression -> (Epigenetic reprogramming & optimized culture conditions) -> Enhanced HNF4α expression via CRISPR activation -> Reactivation of hepatocyte differentiation -> Restoration of mature hepatic transcriptome and increased CYP levels -> Improved in vitro modeling of drug metabolism and toxicity
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a synergistic intervention combining precise HNF4α upregulation (using CRISPR-based activation techniques) with targeted epigenetic modifications (using agents such as 5‑azacytidine and Vitamin C) and optimized culture conditions (including low-density and 3D culture systems to promote tight junction formation) will effectively overcome the dedifferentiation induced by CTNNB1 mutations in HepG2 cells. This multifactorial approach will re-establish the mature hepatocyte transcriptome, restore cytochrome P450 enzyme activity to physiologically relevant levels, and thereby markedly improve the in vitro predictive accuracy for drug metabolism and toxicity studies.
Abstract: In this study, we propose an integrated strategy to re‐differentiate HepG2 cells toward a mature hepatocyte phenotype by concurrently enhancing HNF4α expression and modulating complementary cellular factors. Building upon the established role of HNF4α in hepatic differentiation, our approach leverages CRISPR-based gene activation to precisely upregulate HNF4α, while incorporating targeted epigenetic modifications (via 5‑azacytidine and Vitamin C treatments) and optimizing culture conditions (including low‐density and 3D cell culture systems) to reinforce cell–cell junction dynamics. This multifaceted intervention is designed to reverse the dedifferentiated state induced by CTNNB1 mutations—characterized by impaired HNF4α signaling and low cytochrome P450 expression—and restore mature hepatic functions. Enhanced CYP activity in this reprogrammed phenotype is anticipated to improve the predictive accuracy of in vitro models for drug metabolism and toxicity evaluations.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis focused solely on enhancing HNF4α expression to drive the re-differentiation of HepG2 cells and restore CYP activity. In our revised hypothesis, we retain the central role of HNF4α but explicitly incorporate additional causal steps highlighted by contemporary evidence: (1) correcting the downstream effects of CTNNB1 mutation and impaired HNF4α signaling via complementary epigenetic modulation; (2) optimizing cell culture conditions to enhance tight junction formation, as indicated by cell density effects; and (3) utilizing CRISPR-based gene activation to finely control HNF4α levels. These augmentations address the multifactorial nature of hepatocyte differentiation and provide a more robust, technologically advanced strategy for restoring mature hepatic function in HepG2 cells.
